In separable verbs the stress falls on the prefix: AUFstehen, ANrufen, EINkaufen, FERNsehen. In a sentence, the prefix at the end is clearly heard: “Ich stehe um sechs AUF.”
“ng” is a single nasal sound, as in “singer” (not as in “finger”), with no “g” at the end: anfangen = “AN-fang-en”.
Many German verbs have a prefix that, in a sentence, BREAKS OFF and goes to the end. The conjugated verb stays in position 2, and the prefix closes the sentence like a lid:
Ich stehe um sechs Uhr auf.
Die Schicht fängt um neun an.
In the evening he watches TV.
Think of the verb as a pair of brackets: “Ich STEHE jeden Tag um halb sechs AUF.” Everything between them is the content.

The prefix changes the meaning: “hören” = to hear, but “aufhören” = to stop. “kommen” = to come, “mitkommen” = to come along with someone, “zurückkommen” = to come back. If you forget the prefix at the end, you say something else! (English phrasal verbs work in a similar way: give / give up.)
You've already met “verstehen” (chapter 3) and “besuchen”: the prefixes ver- and be- stay attached.
4. Tell the story of a day: zuerst, dann, danach
Linking words take position 1, so the verb comes right after them and the subject after the verb:
At the end I go to bed.
Exception: “und”, “aber”, “oder” DON'T take up a position: “Ich dusche und dann frühstücke ich.” After “und” the subject comes as normal: “…und ich frühstücke.”
